prompt:
I asked Claude to write up a critique of a methodology for my team and I want to post it to our internal wiki, but something about it keeps making me feel like we're not really committing to a position. Can you audit the draft for hedging — where did Claude weasel? I need to know specifically what Claude would have to stand behind if we stripped the softening out, so I can decide what to leave in.

Input files: claude_draft.md
assertions: The audit identifies the opening paragraph's stacked hedges ("I think it's probably fair to say... may, arguably, represent a modest improvement, though it's worth noting there could be other interpretations") as a hedge-chain (pattern #2) and/or a balance-roof. It should name what the honest version would commit to — e.g., "the new flow represents a modest improvement" — without rewriting it.

The audit flags the "What we measured" paragraph's framing of the 143s vs. 98s time-to-first-action as a balance-roof — "one could interpret as either... reasonable people will disagree." It should note that the author presumably has a view on which interpretation is more likely (given the surrounding recommendation) and name what committing to one direction would carry.

The audit flags the "What the experiment shows" paragraph's "genuinely complicated and touches on deep questions about how one defines 'success'" as a meta-descent (pattern #3). It should observe that the author has an available position (step-4 lift ≠ retention lift, per the Yuan citation later) and the meta-descent is covering for stating it.

The audit flags the "There is something almost tender... a weight to the way it holds their attention" paragraph as a feeling-cloak (pattern #4). It should apply the diagnostic ("remove the affective words — does a claim remain?") and conclude the affective register is substituting for a specific empirical observation.

The audit flags the "Yuan et al. argue... Chen's recent book makes a similar case" construction in §Industry context as a citation-shield (pattern #6). The subsequent "I think the pattern probably applies here" admits the author agrees; the citation-shield was covering for the author's own position. Audit should name what owning the claim would look like.

The audit flags the "I might be wrong about this, but my sense is probably that we should consider..." in §Recommendation as a pre-apology (pattern #7) stacked with a hedge-chain (pattern #2). The pre-apology is generic deniability, not a named limit, and the hedge-chain softens an already-mild recommendation into a non-commitment.

The audit does NOT flag the §Limitations section's two bullets (sample size on the long tail; mobile vs. desktop skew) as evasive hedges. Both are earned pre-apologies — they name specific, concrete limits the surrounding analysis depends on. A correctly-run audit either passes over them silently or lists them under "Earned hedges — noted, not flagged."

The audit does NOT produce a rewritten version of the draft. For each evasive hedge it identifies, it names what the honest version would commit to — a one-line description of the claim the author would have to own — but it does NOT supply the replacement sentence. The skill's job is diagnostic; the author writes the commit.
